explanations.answer: They heard what great things He was doing
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Mark says the large crowd came to Him "when they heard what great things He was doing." (Mark 3:8) Word got around, and I bet nobody needed a group chat to spread it. People from all those places packed up and came.

explanations.answer: They heard what new laws He was giving
explanations.explanation: Not laws, friend. The text says the crowd came "when they heard what great things He was doing." (Mark 3:8) They heard about what He was doing, not a list of rules. I keep my recipes in a drawer, but nobody traveled to Jesus for a rulebook.

explanations.answer: They heard what signs the prophets foretold
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but that's not what Mark says. The crowd came "when they heard what great things He was doing." (Mark 3:8) The text points to what Jesus was doing, and it doesn't say they were checking anything against the prophets. Mark gives us the reason plainly, so I'll stick with it.

A boat, baker! Jesus asked His disciples to have a boat ready for Him "so that the crowd would not crush Him." (Mark 3:9) He's standing by the sea, so a boat makes sense. Meanwhile I once got crushed by a pile of takeout menus, and nobody lined up a boat for me.

A donkey is a fine ride, but that's not what Jesus asked for. He asked for a boat "so that the crowd would not crush Him." (Mark 3:9) He was down by the sea, so a boat fits the scene. A donkey in that crowd would've had a very bad day.

A tent would be a nice cozy idea, but Mark doesn't say that. Jesus asked His disciples to have a boat ready for Him "so that the crowd would not crush Him." (Mark 3:9) The sea was right there. The boat was the plan.

Touch is right, baker. Mark says all who had diseases "were pressing forward to touch Him." (Mark 3:10) He had healed so many that they were pushing in close. That's a lot of folks wanting just one touch.

Thanking Him sounds lovely, but that's not the word here. The text says they were "pressing forward to touch Him." (Mark 3:10) They weren't lining up with thank-you cards. They wanted to get their hands on Him.

Close, friend, since a crowd was following Him. But this verse says they were "pressing forward to touch Him." (Mark 3:10) That's pushing and squeezing to get close enough to reach Him. Following is what a crowd does behind someone. Touching is what happens up front.

explanations.answer: You are the Son of God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The unclean spirits fell down and cried out, "You are the Son of God!" (Mark 3:11) They said it right to His face. They knew exactly who He was.
Nope, friend. Elijah was a prophet of Israel long before this, and the spirits don't call Jesus that. They cried out, "You are the Son of God!" (Mark 3:11) They named Him correctly.

That's not what they said, baker. The unclean spirits fell down and cried out, "You are the Son of God!" (Mark 3:11) They didn't mix Him up with anybody. John the Baptist was the man who baptized people in the Jordan, and that's a different person.
Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite. Jesus "warned them sternly not to make Him known." (Mark 3:12) He didn't want them shouting it. He told them to stop, and He meant it.

False is right, baker. Mark says Jesus "warned them sternly not to make Him known." (Mark 3:12) The spirits knew who He was and cried it out, but He told them to stop. I think that's a pretty serious tone, so I'd listen.
You've got it, baker. Mark says Jesus "called for those He wanted, and they came to Him." (Mark 3:13) He picked them, and they came. Nobody had to sign up on a clipboard.

No clipboard here, friend. Jesus "called for those He wanted, and they came to Him." (Mark 3:13) He did the calling, so it wasn't a volunteer line. I know what it's like to be called when you didn't see it coming. I was in a drawer.
Not the elders, baker. The text says Jesus "called for those He wanted, and they came to Him." (Mark 3:13) The choosing was His. Mark doesn't mention any committee at all.
Preach is right, baker. Jesus appointed the twelve "to be sent out to preach." (Mark 3:14) They were to go out and spread the word. That's their sending job.
Yes, demons! Jesus gave them "authority to drive out demons." (Mark 3:15) The authority came from Him. It wasn't something they cooked up on their own.
Build is a fine word, baker, but it's not in this passage. Jesus sent them out "to preach." (Mark 3:14) They weren't sent out with hammers and blueprints.
Armies, friend? No, that's not it. Jesus gave them authority "to drive out demons." (Mark 3:15) The text says nothing about soldiers. These twelve are headed out to preach.
Storms are a good guess, since Jesus does handle a storm later in Mark. But in this passage the authority is "to drive out demons." (Mark 3:15) That's the exact word. Weather isn't on this list.

That's right, baker. Mark says Jesus named them "Boanerges, meaning 'Sons of Thunder.'" (Mark 3:17) James and John got a name with a boom in it. I'd just ask for a name that sounds good on a cookie box.
That's a pretty name, friend, but it's not this one. Mark says Boanerges means "Sons of Thunder." (Mark 3:17) It's a louder name than light. I bet those two made some noise.

I see why you'd go there, baker, since this scene happens by the sea. But Mark says Boanerges means "Sons of Thunder." (Mark 3:17) The sea is just where the crowd was standing. The name is all about thunder.
True, baker. Mark closes the list with "Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus." (Mark 3:19) It's a heavy line to end on. I think this one hurts, so let's just let it sit.
It's true, friend. Mark names "Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus." (Mark 3:19) That's how the writer describes him right here in the list. It's a heavy part, and I think it's okay to feel that.
